speaker_role: student (self-described Stanford admit narrating from personal experience)
commercial_incentive: none evident; personal YouTube channel, not a consulting business
key_insights: Recommends 10-15 schools total structured as an 'upside-down triangle': 1-2 safety, 2-4 target, and the remainder reach, since many reach-school admit rates are under 5%
Argues elite, expensive-looking schools often have the most generous need-based aid due to large endowments, citing his own experience where Stanford was cheaper than his in-state options
Recommends researching a target major's department strength directly on the department's own website (faculty, class sizes, opportunities) rather than relying only on aggregate ranking sites
Advises against building an identity around a single 'dream school,' noting students are often emotionally devastated by denial from a school they over-invested in
Suggests weighing non-academic fit factors (campus size, social/party scene, school spirit, climate, housing) as seriously as academic fit when building a list
specific_numbers_or_facts: Presenter personally applied to 27 schools but recommends 10-15 for most students
States that at the time, Stanford waived tuition entirely for families earning under $100,000/year (per presenter)
notable_or_distinctive: first-person account from a student admitted to Stanford despite it being entirely outside his original list and region, used to argue against self-limiting based on assumed cost or fit before researching aid
reliability_notes: single student's personal experience/opinion, not an admissions professional; specific claims (e.g., Stanford's income cutoff) may be dated or oversimplified and should be checked against current published policy
